headlines.story: FAYETTEVILLE, Ark. -- — KJ Jackson threw for 188 yards and two touchdowns and Arkansas took advantage of four turnovers by South Carolina to beat the No. 17 Gamecocks 34-6 on Saturday night. It was the Razorbacks’ first Southeastern Conference victory at home since Nov. 5, 2024 against Tennessee, which was also the last time Arkansas (4-6, 2-5) beat a ranked opponent. South Carolina’s loss snapped a four-game winning streak. Both of Jackson’s touchdown passes came in the second quarter as Arkansas built a 17-0 halftime lead. He found Chris Marshall for a 23-yard score for the team’s first touchdown and then connected with Antonio Jordan for a 28-yard score on the next drive. South Carolina’s offense struggled without starting quarterback LaNorris Sellers, who did not play after injuring his ankle in the team’s win over Texas A&M Nov. 7. Cutter Woods played the entire game, going 24 of 43 passing for 271 yards with three interceptions. The Gamecocks (6-4, 4-4) still had chances, but went just 1 for 5 in the red zone with a lost fumble, a missed field goal and an interception ending three of those drives. The fumble came on the team’s second trip inside the Arkansas 20 when the Gamecocks attempted a reverse and lost the ball on the exchange. The Razorbacks recovered at the 18 then drove 82 yards on 11 plays for Marshall’s score. Jabree Coleman’s 3-yard touchdown run put South Carolina on the board early in the second half. After forcing a punt, the Gamecocks entered Arkansas territory again, but Woods’ pass intended for Donovan Murph was intercepted by Joker Johnson, who ran 63 yards for a score. Johnson intercepted Woods again early in the fourth quarter and Ben Bogle picked off the South Carolina quarterback on the next drive, as well. Johnson finished with two interceptions, a forced fumble and led the team with eight tackles. Jackson went 15 of 24 through the air and added 46 yards rushing for Arkansas. Marshall caught four passes for 63 yards and a touchdown while Jordan caught four passes for 62 yards and a touchdown. Sutton Smith capped the Razorbacks’ scoring with a 7-yard touchdown run with 1:50 left. South Carolina, which entered the game ranked 20th in FBS averaging 205.4 yards per game, picked up a season-low 98 on the ground on 30 attempts. Sellers leads the team with 637 yards and seven touchdowns and starting running back Matt Fuller, who ran for 530 yards in the team’s first eight games, was lost for the season in the team’s Halloween win against Oklahoma. The takeaway After a miserable start to the season, the Razorbacks have looked better over most of the last month in coach Ryan Silverfield’s first season with two wins and a one-possession loss. South Carolina coach Shane Beamer’s campaign to extricate himself from the hot seat took a serious turn for the worse with the loss. The Gamecocks have just No. 1 Georgia and rival Clemson remaining on their schedule. Losses in both would result in a disappointing .500 season. Up Next Arkansas plays at No. 8 Texas on Saturday. South Carolina hosts No. 1 Georgia on Saturday. ------ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here. Visit the Top 25 here and see AP’s full college football coverage here.

headlines.story: TULSA, Okla. -- — Baylor Haynes threw for 309 yards and two touchdowns and Tulsa never trailed in a 38-21 win over Florida Atlantic on Saturday night to become eligible for a bowl game. Javon Ross had 163 yards on six receptions, Damari Alston ran for 92 yards on 11 carries and scored a touchdown, and Trequan Jones scored twice on the ground for Tulsa (6-4, 3-3 American Conference). Caden Veltkamp threw for 340 yards and two touchdowns, completing 32 of 58 passes for FAU (6-4, 3-3). Haynes threw a 5-yard touchdown to Jimmy Calloway with 1:47 left in the first quarter for the game's first score. Tulsa made it 14-0 early in the second when Haynes threw a 9-yard score to Calloway. FAU responded on the ensuing drive when Veltkamp threw a 7-yard touchdown to Easton Messer with 10:13 before halftime. But less than a minute later, Jones ran 78 yards for a touchdown to put Tulsa back up by two touchdowns. Brady Tillman III's 6-yard touchdown run with 4:26 before halftime brought the Owls within a touchdown but they never got closer. Tulsa has won three of its last four games while averaging almost 43 points. Up next Florida Atlantic: Hosts South Florida on Saturday. Tulsa: Hosts Charlotte on Saturday. ------ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here. Visit the Top 25 here and see AP’s full college football coverage here.

headlines.story: BLACKSBURG, Va. -- — Micah Ford rushed for 149 yards and three touchdowns and Stanford’s defense forced three turnovers to lead the Cardinal to a 40-22 victory over Virginia Tech on Saturday. The Cardinal (5-5, 3-4 Atlantic Coast Conference), who scored their most points in an ACC game since joining the league, snapped a 15-game road losing streak, which was the longest in school history and had been the longest active streak in FBS. Stanford’s last road win came Sept. 20, 2024 at Syracuse. Virginia Tech (6-4, 3-4) entered the game as 15.5-point favorites according to Sportsbook, but the Hokies turned the ball over three times in the first half, fell behind 21-0, and never recovered in losing their second consecutive game. The Cardinal scored 14 points off Virginia Tech turnovers and scored on its final four possessions of the first half to lead 24-7 at halftime. Stanford safety Charlie Eckhardt caused all three turnovers, intercepting two passes and forcing a fumble. Eckhardt’s second interception led to Stanford’s first score, a 16-yard touchdown run by quarterback Davis Warren for a 7-0 lead late in the first quarter. Eckhardt forced a fumble by Virginia Tech’s Que’Sean Brown that was recovered by Jay Green led to a 5-yard touchdown run by Ford that gave the Cardinal a 21-0 lead with 7:40 left in the first half. Ford also scored on runs of 3 and 2 yards, the latter coming with 8:27 left in the game that gave the Cardinal a 37-14 lead. Ford has rushed for more than 100 yards in three of the Cardinal’s past four games. Jeffrey Overton Jr. led the Hokies with 107 yards rushing and a touchdown. Takeaways Stanford: The Cardinal’s defense entered the game ranked last in the ACC in scoring defense (37.3 per game), total defense (454.1 yards per game), and total sacks (six). But that unit sacked Virginia Tech’s Ethan Grunkemeyer five times, held the Hokies to just 398 total yards, and played arguably its best game against a Power 4 team this season. Virginia Tech: This was a dreadful home performance by the Hokies in all phases. The offense turned the ball over and couldn’t protect Grunkemeyer, and the defense now has given up 91 points and more than 1,000 yards in the past two games. Up next Stanford: Plays at California on Saturday. Virginia Tech: Plays at Miami on Saturday. ------ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here. headlines.story:
Few coaches can have a greater impact on their team than those in college football, where the duties of a head coach read more like that of a CEO: recruiting and developing personnel, constructing weekly and yearlong game plans, working with key stakeholders inside and outside the university and generally serving as the face of the program. It's a demanding job, which makes each win all the more impressive. It's also why many of the winningest coaches across college football history have literal statues built in their honor -- including many coaches on this list.

In March 2026, Lou Holtz died at the age of 89. Holtz had a record of 249-132-7 over his head coaching career.

Here's an inside look at the 25 best college football coaches of all time ranked by official wins at FBS schools. 

*Active coaches are denoted with an asterisk

1. Joe Paterno, 409 wins

In his 46 years at Happy Valley, the longtime Penn State boss finished his career with a 409-136-3 record (.749). He led the Nittany Lions to a record 37 bowl appearances and 24 wins -- including two national championships (1982, 1986) and five undefeated seasons.

2. Bobby Bowden, 346 wins

Bowden spent the first six years of his FBS coaching career at West Virginia (42-26), but he's best known for his 34 years at Florida State, where he led the Seminoles to a 304-97-4 record (.756) with two national championships (1993, 1999) and 12 ACC titles. They also finished in the top five of the AP poll in a record 14 straight seasons.

3. Bear Bryant, 323 wins

Long considered the greatest college football coach of all time, Paul "Bear" Bryant was the winningest coach in the sport's history when he retired in 1982, and his six national championships at Alabama were the most all time until Nick Saban won his seventh in 2020. Bryant's all-time win percentage (.780) still ranks in the top 20.

4. Pop Warner, 318 wins

Few coaches have had a greater impact on football than Warner, who helped advance the fundamentals of the sport in the early 20th century and was key to the development of the youth program named after him. He also did plenty of winning: Warner claimed four national titles at Pittsburgh and Stanford, and his teams won at least 60% of their games in 35 of his 44 seasons.

5. Amos Alonzo Stagg, 314 wins

In 41 years at Chicago, Stagg led his team to four undefeated seasons and two national championships (1905, 1913; the NCAA site lists Harvard as the champions, but the school claims the championship). His entire coaching career lasted 71 years -- the longest in college football history -- and he's one of only four people elected to the College Football Hall of Fame as both a player and coach. He was also elected to the Basketball Hall of Fame in 1959.

6. Nick Saban, 292 wins

While Saban may not be first on this list, he's considered by many as the greatest college football coach of all time. In 28 seasons, Saban won a record seven national championships -- six at Alabama and one at LSU. 

7. Mack Brown, 288 wins

Brown was elected to the College Football Hall of Fame in 2018 before returning to North Carolina, where he ranks as the school's all-time leader in wins (113). He also ranks second in all-time wins at Texas (158), where he led the Longhorns to their fourth national title in 2005. In November 2024, UNC announced that Brown would not return as head coach in 2025. 

8. LaVell Edwards, 257 wins

Edwards spent his entire 29-year career at BYU, where he led the team to a 257-101-3 record (.716) and coached the Cougars to their only national championship in 1984. He also coached the school's lone Heisman Trophy winner (Ty Detmer) in 1990, and he remains the only 100-win coach in BYU history.

9. Tom Osborne, 255 wins

While other coaches on this list have won more games, none have been more efficient than Osborne, whose .836 win percentage is the sixth best in college football history and by far the best of any FBS coach with at least 200 wins. The Hall of Fame coach led Nebraska to three national titles in 25 years and posted a 60-3 record over his final five seasons.

10. Lou Holtz, 249 wins

Holtz is best known for his 11 seasons at Notre Dame, where he led the Fighting Irish to a stellar 100-30-2 record (.765) and a perfect 12-0 record in 1988 to earn consensus national championship honors. Yet that was just one stop across 33 seasons for Holtz, who remains the only coach to lead six different teams to bowl games.

11. Frank Beamer, 238 wins

Beamer spent his entire FBS coaching career at Virginia Tech, where his brand of "Beamer Ball" -- which emphasized contributions in all three phases -- helped turn the program around after his arrival in 1987. Beamer led the Hokies to seven conference titles and their lone national championship appearance in 1999, one of 25 winning seasons in his 29-year tenure.

12. Bo Schembechler, 234 wins

It's hard to find a more beloved coach than Schembechler, who remains the winningest coach of college football's all-time winningest program. In 21 seasons at Michigan, the legendary coach led the Wolverines to 13 Big Ten titles and finished ranked in the AP Poll in all but one season. He also won 11 games against Ohio State, the second most by any Michigan coach.

13. Hayden Fry, 232 wins

Fry may not have the name recognition of some of the other coaches on this list, but the Hall of Fame coach made his impact felt across 37 seasons at SMU, North Texas and Iowa. Fry helped integrate the Southwest Conference in 1965 and turned around the Iowa football program in 1979. His coaching tree was one of the most prolific of all time.

14. Steve Spurrier, 228 wins

One of four people elected to the College Football Hall of Fame as a player and coach, Spurrier won the Heisman Trophy in 1966 and posted a winning record in 23 of 26 seasons at Duke, Florida and South Carolina. "The Head Ball Coach" led the Gators to a national championship in 1996 and was a nine-time conference coach of the year -- seven times in the SEC and twice in the ACC.

15. Woody Hayes, 219 wins

While Hayes' coaching career was marred by his infamous punch in the 1978 Gator Bowl, it's hard to dispute his accolades on the field. In 28 seasons at Ohio State, Hayes won three major poll national champions and 13 Big Ten titles with four undefeated seasons, and his Buckeyes finished ranked in the top 10 a whopping 15 times.

16. Kirk Ferentz*, 217 wins

While Hayden Fry helped establish a winning culture at Iowa, Ferentz has since surpassed the legendary coach atop the school's all-time leaderboard. In September 2025, he surpassed Woody Hayes for the most all-time wins as a head coach at a Big Ten program.

17. Bill Snyder, 215 wins

Nobody is more synonymous with Kansas State football than Snyder, who turned around arguably the worst team in college football history in his 27 seasons in Manhattan. After 13 seasons as an assistant under Hayden Fry, Snyder inherited a Wildcats team riding a 27-game winless streak and led them to a 215-117-1 record (.647), including two Big 12 titles and their first nine bowl wins in program history.

18. Don Nehlen, 202 wins

After serving as an assistant under Bo Schembechler in the late 1970s, Nehlen went on to become one of just 18 coaches to win 200 games at the FBS level. Much of that came in his 21 years at West Virginia, where he led the Mountaineers to a 149-93-4 record (.614) and two undefeated regular seasons.

19. Vince Dooley, 201 wins

Georgia is currently in the midst of its greatest run in program history. No coach has led the Bulldogs to more wins than Dooley, who posted just one losing record in his 25 years in Athens. He also guided the school to six SEC titles and a national championship in 1980, earning him national coach of the year honors and his 4th SEC Coach of the Year award.

20. Dan McGugin, 197 wins

It's hard to win at Vanderbilt, a school that has enjoyed a winning record in just four of the past 48 seasons. That makes it all the more impressive what McGugin was able to accomplish in his 30-year run with the Commodores: winning 76.2% of his games -- and 11 conference titles, before being inducted in the inaugural College Football Hall of Fame class in 1951.

headlines.headline: Jackson Arnold rallies UNLV past No. 23 New Mexico, 21-17
headlines.description: — Jackson Arnold threw a long fourth-quarter touchdown pass and ran for another score and UNLV beat No. 23 New Mexico 21-17 on Saturday night, spoiling the Lobos' first home game in The Associated Press poll.
headlines.linkText: Jackson Arnold rallies UNLV past No. 23 New Mexico, 21-17
headlines.story: ALBUQUERQUE, N.M. -- — Jackson Arnold threw a long fourth-quarter touchdown pass and ran for another score and UNLV beat No. 23 New Mexico 21-17 on Saturday night, spoiling the Lobos' first home game in The Associated Press poll. Arnold threw for 201 yards and two touchdowns and rushed for 98 yards to help UNLV (6-4, 4-2 Mountain West) beat the Lobos (8-2, 5-1) on the road for the fifth straight time. The Rebels fell behind 14-0 as New Mexico relied on its power rushing game and stout defense. Scottre Humphrey went over from 3 yards in the first quarter for the Lobos, and Cade Keith caught a 9-yard touchdown pass from Toa Fa’avae in the second quarter, but New Mexico could not quite generate enough offense the rest of the way. And late in the first half, Arnold found Keyan Burnett for an 18-yard scoring pass that set the stage for the second half. In the fourth quarter, Arnold threw a 43-yard touchdown pass to cut it to 17-14 with 11:40 left, then took a quarterback draw 44 yards for 21-17 lead with 7:26 to go. The takeaway UNLV: Remained in contention for the conference title. New Mexico: The loss will almost certainly end New Mexico’s time in the rankings after two weeks, but the Lobos remain a front-runner for the conference championship. Up next UNLV: At San Jose on Saturday. New Mexico: At Wyoming on Friday night. ------ Sign up for Top 25 poll alerts here, visit the Top 25 here and see AP’s full college football coverage here

headlines.story: JACKSONVILLE, Ala. -- — Ethan Croley finished with 20 points and 17 rebounds to help Jacksonville State hold on for a 71-68 victory over UAB on Saturday night. Leon Horner scored 17 for the Gamecocks (2-2) and Jordan Stiemke added 11 points. Justyn Fernandez led the way for the Blazers (2-2) with 15 points and three steals. Salim London added 14 points and seven rebounds, while Jeremy Elyzee scored 13. Croley scored 12 points in the first half for Jacksonville State, which led 35-30 at the break. The Gamecocks used a 12-0 second-half run to pull away from a 51-51 tie. ------ The Associated Press created this story using technology provided by Data Skrive and data from Sportradar.
